title: SDK integration walkthrough - Stellar Commerce
summary: Walkthrough of Redwood SDKs (Python & TypeScript), authentication options (API key, SSO, service principal), environment setup, and quickstarts. Reviewed hosted vs dedicated vs private VPC options, latency/cost tradeoffs, and security compliance (SOC2, encryption, KMS). Agreed to run a short pilot to validate latency for checkout flows; Redwood to send security pack, quickstart repo, and pricing. Next call to schedule benchmarks week of 11/9.
topics: Auth patterns: API keys vs SSO vs service account
Env setup: local dev, CI, secrets management
transcript:
Header: 2026-11-03 16:00 PT | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Maya Chen, Diego Alvarez (Redwood); Priya Singh, Marcus Lee, Aria Patel, Sam Torres (Stellar)

Auto-summary: Quick SDK demo + setup, security discussion, next steps to pilot.

00:00 Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account, joining with Diego our SE. How's every- how's everyones afternoon?
00:12 Priya Singh: Hi Maya, hi Diego. Afternoon, busy day but good, thanks.
00:18 Diego Alvarez: Cool, we'll keep it focused. We'll do a 10-minute walkthrough of the Python and TypeScript SDKs, auth and env setup, then leave time for questions and security stuff.
00:30 Marcus Lee: Sounds good, we're most interested in low-latency inference for our checkout recommender and how to run this in our VPC.
00:38 Diego Alvarez: Great, we'll highlight hosted vs dedicated vs private and how the SDKs change (mostly config).
00:47 Maya Chen: Quick qualification: what's your current stack for inference and hosting? Marcus?
00:52 Marcus Lee: We're on GCP, Kubernetes, use a mix of in-house models (TensorFlow) and some API calls to 3rd-party vendors. We do have a latency SLA of sub-120ms p95 for recommender in the fast path, but can tolerate more for batch tasks.
01:10 Priya Singh: Security wise, we need SOC2 alignments, SSO/SAML for console access, and KMS integration for keys. Also data residency in EU for some customers.
01:25 Diego Alvarez: That's pretty standard. Redwood supports SSO/SAML, RBAC, and KMS/HSM integrations for private deployments; hosted customers can use Redwood-managed KMS with optional contract terms for suid. For EU residency we can pin region to eu-west and also dedicated/private if needed.
01:45 Sam Torres: Any competitors you see commonly?
01:48 Maya Chen: Customers usually evaluate [Redacted], BigCloudAI, and self-hosted clusters.
01:55 Marcus Lee: Ok, show the SDKs.
02:05 Diego Alvarez: Alright, switching to the screen. First the Python quickstart: pip install redwood-inference (note: this is a transcript, package names described verbally). Example:
02:20 Diego Alvarez: from redwood_inference import Client
02:25 Diego Alvarez: client = Client(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
02:31 Diego Alvarez: resp = client.generate(model='gpt-small', prompt='Recommend three complementary items for a running shoe', max_tokens=64)
02:42 Priya Singh: Does the SDK handle streaming? Can we stream tokens to our frontend?
02:48 Diego Alvarez: Yes, streaming is first-class; in Python we have a stream() iterator and in TypeScript we expose an async iterable and streaming through EventSource for browsers.
03:05 Marcus Lee: How do we manage keys in CI? We use GitLab CI.
03:10 Maya Chen: We recommend storing secrets in your CI provider (GitLab CI variables), and for private deployments you can use service principal with short-lived tokens via our STS. We'll include a sample GitLab job in the quickstart repo.
03:28 Aria Patel: For on-prem or VPC, how is egress handled? We have strict firewall rules.
03:33 Diego Alvarez: For private, the control plane can be customer-managed; data plane can be deployed on your VPC with no outbound egress to public internet. We do an on-prem package for air-gapped environments too but that's a separate enterprise agreement.
03:50 Priya Singh: Can you show TypeScript example?
03:55 Diego Alvarez: npm i @redwood/inference then:
04:00 Diego Alvarez: import { RedwoodClient } from '@redwood/inference'
04:05 Diego Alvarez: const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY })
04:12 Diego Alvarez: const resp = await client.generate({ model: 'gpt-small', prompt: '...' })
04:20 Marcus Lee: Are there official Next.js or Node serverless examples?
04:24 Maya Chen: Yep, quickstarts include Next.js edge and serverless examples, and we've seen customers use serverless for lower traffic endpoints and dedicated for high-throughput real-time.
04:40 Sam Torres: Pricing question: how much difference between hosted and dedicated?
04:44 Maya Chen: Hosted is pay-as-you-go; Dedicated is reserved capacity with better unit economics at scale and predictable latency. We'll send a pricing sheet tailored to your projected traffic.
05:00 Priya Singh: About latency: you mentioned batching and KV cache — can that impact p95?
05:06 Diego Alvarez: Yes, automatic batching improves throughput but can add a small headroom to latency; Redwood Optimize suggests batching policies per route. For KV cache/prefix cache it reduces tokens and cost for repeated contexts, improves tail latency for repeated sessions but does add some cache lookup overhead — tradeoffs we can tune.
05:35 Marcus Lee: Do we need to change model architecture for quantization?
05:39 Diego Alvarez: Usually no changes required. Quantization profiles are applied during model onboarding; for private deployments we can offer int8 or int4 variants.
06:00 Priya Singh: Security details — audit logs and retention?
06:04 Maya Chen: We provide audit logs for all admin actions and can stream logs to your SIEM via secure forwarder; retention is configurable for Dedicated/Private. Hosted default retention is 90 days; enterprise add-on for longer retention.
06:25 Aria Patel: KMS integration?
06:28 Diego Alvarez: We integrate with cloud KMS (GCP KMS, AWS KMS) and support HSM for private deployments. Keys can be customer-managed.
06:40 Priya Singh: Any certifications?
06:42 Maya Chen: We are SOC2 Type II certified; ISO in progress. We'll attach the SOC2 report in the security pack.
07:00 Marcus Lee: For the SDK, how does retry/backoff and idempotency work?
07:05 Diego Alvarez: SDK includes automatic retry with exponential backoff for transient 5xx, and idempotency tokens for request dedupe. You'll be able to configure those in client options.
07:20 Sam Torres: Ok can you demo a quick local env setup?
07:25 Diego Alvarez: Sure. Steps: 1) create API key in Console -> API Keys -> new key; 2) export REDWOOD_API_KEY in your shell or use direnv; 3) pip install redwood-inference; 4) run the sample. I'll paste a link to the quickstart repo in the notes.
08:00 Priya Singh: Is there a CLI?
08:03 Maya Chen: We have a CLI for dev workflows (redwoodctl) that can run local proxies for private connectors and manage keys; we'll include CLI docs.
08:15 Aria Patel: Observability: token-level cost breakdown?
08:19 Diego Alvarez: Yep, Console provides per-route token cost, latency histograms, per-model breakdowns and trace ids you can forward to your tracing system.
08:35 Marcus Lee: For the pilot, what's the minimal setup?
08:38 Maya Chen: For a pilot we suggest hosted with a dedicated model variant and a scoped traffic test — that gives you speed to evaluate latency and cost without provisioning GPUs. If you're happy, we can migrate to Dedicated with reserved capacity.
09:00 Priya Singh: Data residency — can we keep EU only?
09:03 Diego Alvarez: Yes, we can pin regions and for strict residency we recommend Dedicated or Private.
09:15 Sam Torres: Any gotchas for web clients?
09:18 Diego Alvarez: Browser keys should be proxied via backend with short-lived tokens; don't embed long-lived API keys in the frontend. We provide examples using the server to fetch ephemeral tokens and then connect to streaming endpoints.
09:40 Marcus Lee: Ok let's talk timeline — we want a pilot in two weeks.
09:43 Maya Chen: Sounds feasible; we'll need a small scope doc from you with endpoints and traffic expectations; Diego can take technical details.
10:00 Diego Alvarez: I'll follow up with a benchmark template so you can run p95 tests and we can help interpret.

--- (mid call, more Q&A, a few transcription errors / filler) ---
20:12 Speaker 1: uh so like if we do the private path, do we need to change the models?
20:18 Diego Alvarez: No, model artifacts move but you can choose quantized builds, nothing to change in your inference calls.
25:40 Priya Singh: Sorry I'm on phone audio — there's a little drop.
25:45 Maya Chen: No problem, we can send the recording.
30:00 Diego Alvarez: Demo conclusion, I'll paste CLI and repo links in the notes.
40:10 Marcus Lee: Re: competitors, we ran some perf tests with BigCloudAI and saw slightly higher tail latency for equivalent configs — happy to share those results.
41:00 Maya Chen: Great, we can help run comparative benchmarks too.
45:20 Priya Singh: One more question on RBAC and SAML groups mapping to Console roles?
45:25 Diego Alvarez: We map SAML attributes to RBAC groups and Console roles; we'll include an example SAML mapping YAML in the security pack.
50:00 Maya Chen: Okay let's recap next steps.
50:06 Maya Chen: Diego will send quickstart repo, benchmark template, and sample GitLab CI job; I'll send security pack (SOC2, SSO guides, KMS notes) and pricing; Priya will send pilot scope and endpoints.
50:20 Priya Singh: Yep we'll send scope doc by Friday.
50:25 Sam Torres: Thanks everyone.
50:30 Maya Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up with calendar invite to schedule benchmark session next week.
50:38 Recording stopped.
